wrest

REST -- from Old English wraestan ('to twist, wrench'); the same Germanic root behind wrestle. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To wrest is to forcefully take something away from someone's grasp or control.

Corporate raiders spent months trying to wrest control of the family-owned company through a hostile takeover.

Example

After years of backroom deals, the junior senator finally managed to wrest control of the committee away from its longtime chairman.

That forceful, often difficult act of taking something away from someone who is holding onto it tightly -- whether a physical object or a position of power -- is exactly what it means to wrest something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wrench: To wrench is to pull or twist something suddenly and violently -- a stuck drawer, a jammed lid. To wrest shares that violent pull but adds an opponent: you wrest a thing away from a person's determined grip, working it loose against real resistance.

grab: Grab is the plain, everyday word for taking hold of something quickly, with no struggle implied -- you grab keys, a snack, a seat. To wrest is far more effortful: something is wrested only from a grip that fights to keep it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

surrender: to give up control or possession of something

relinquish: to formally give up a right or possession

Where it sits · how forcefully it is taken

snatch → wrest → seize

snatch vs. wrest: Snatch is milder than wrest: a snatch is over in an instant, taking something before anyone can resist at all, while to wrest is to fight a determined grip and force the thing loose.

seize vs. wrest: Seize is more forceful than wrest: to wrest is to drag one prized thing free of a single opponent's grip, while to seize is to take hold of something completely and at once -- an army seizes a whole bridge in a single stroke.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — wraest-: to twist, wrench (Old English (wraestan))

Put it together: Wrest comes from Old English wraestan, 'to twist or wrench' -- the very same Germanic root behind wrestle, which describes the physical twisting and grappling of a struggle for control.

Use the root in a new word: wrestle: The two brothers wrestled over the last slice of pizza until it ended up on the floor.

Root Check

Word Choice

Wrest almost always implies real resistance -- you wrest something away from someone who is actively holding on, unlike simply taking or receiving something freely offered.
